6: ---
7: 
8: # Codex CLI Orchestrator - Cross-AI Task Delegation
9: 
10: > **CRITICAL — SELF-INVOCATION PROHIBITED**
11: >
12: > This skill dispatches to the OpenAI CLI binary (`codex`). If the agent currently reading this skill is itself running inside Codex (detection signals listed in the self-invocation guard in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md)), the skill MUST refuse to load and return the documented error message instead of generating any `codex` invocation.
13: >
14: > A running CLI skill never dispatches itself. The cli-X skills are for **cross-AI delegation only** — never self-invocation.
15: 
16: Orchestrate OpenAI's Codex CLI for tasks that benefit from a second AI perspective, real-time web search, deep codebase analysis, built-in code review workflows, or parallel code generation.
17: 
18: **Core Principle**: Use Codex for what it does best. Delegate, validate, integrate. The calling AI stays the conductor.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. WHEN TO USE
23: 
24: ### Activation Triggers
25: 
26: - **Cross-AI Validation** — code review second perspective, security audit alternative analysis, bug detection, `/review` diff-aware workflow.
27: - **Web Research** — current internet info via the top-level `--search` flag (`codex --search exec …`), latest library versions, API changes, community solutions.
28: - **Codebase Architecture Analysis** — onboarding to unfamiliar codebases, cross-file dependency mapping, architecture docs from code.
29: - **Parallel Task Processing** — offloading generation, simultaneous code generations, background docs/test generation.
30: - **Agent-Delegated Tasks** — specialized profile matches (`.codex/agents/*.toml`), session management (resume, fork), multi-strategy planning.
31: - **Specialized Generation** — explicit Codex requests, test suite generation, code translation, batch docs (JSDoc, README, API), visual input via `--image`/`-i`.
32: 
33: ### When NOT to Use
34: 
35: - **You ARE Codex already.** If your runtime is Codex (detection signal: `$CODEX_SESSION_ID` or any `CODEX_*` env var set, `codex` in process ancestry, or `~/.codex/state/<id>/lock` present), this skill refuses to load. Self-invocation creates a circular dispatch loop and burns tokens for no value.
36: - Simple, quick tasks where CLI overhead is not worth it, or tasks needing an immediate response (rate limits may delay).
37: - Context already loaded and understood by the current agent.
38: - Interactive refinement requiring the full-screen TUI (use `codex` directly instead).
39: - Tasks where Codex CLI is not installed.
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 2. SMART ROUTING
44: 
45: The `cli-external-orchestration` hub routes an OpenAI dispatch here: the prompt names Codex, the Codex CLI, `codex exec` or a web-research or second-opinion handoff, and the hub's `cli-codex` mode signal selects this packet.
46: A session already running inside Codex never routes here; the self-invocation guard refuses it.
47: The hub [`ROUTER.md`](../ROUTER.md) names the two leaves a dispatch starts from.
48: Inside this packet the `ALWAYS` tier loads first: `references/cli-reference.md` for the subcommands, flags and sandbox modes, and `assets/prompt-quality-card.md` for the fast-path prompt framework.
49: Intent-mapped references load after those, one set per intent.
50: Read [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) before selecting skill-local resources; open only the matched files.
51: 
52: ---
53: 
54: ## 3. HOW IT WORKS
55: 
56: ### Prerequisites
57: 
58: Install with `npm i -g @openai/codex`, or with `brew install --cask codex`.
59: cli-codex authenticates through **ChatGPT OAuth only**. Run `codex login` and complete the browser flow, which requires a ChatGPT Plus/Pro/Business/Edu/Enterprise account. The skill does not use an OpenAI API key.
60: The ALWAYS-loaded [cli-reference.md](./references/cli-reference.md) holds the full install, auth, flag, sandbox, session and troubleshooting tables. This section keeps only the routing decisions and dispatch-critical gotchas.
61: 
62: ### Execution Ownership
63: 
64: This packet owns user-facing routing, the `command -v codex` availability probe, prompt construction, and the self-invocation guard.
65: Research and review lineages delegate process construction and execution to the already-shipped deep-loop runtime at `../../system-deep-loop/runtime/scripts/fanout-run.cjs`, using executor kind `cli-codex`.
66: That runner accepts only the `research` and `review` loop types, so a single build or doc dispatch uses the child dispatch envelope in [providers-and-models.md](./references/providers-and-models.md) §5.
67: 
68: The runtime is the single Codex execution adapter. Do not add a packet-local wrapper, command builder, or spawn path. Direct `codex exec` snippets below are operator reference and manual-testing examples; research and review lineages use the shared runtime, and a one-shot dispatch uses the child envelope.
69: 
70: ### Provider Auth Pre-Flight (ChatGPT OAuth)
71: 
72: **MANDATORY before any first dispatch in a session.** cli-codex authenticates through ChatGPT OAuth only. If `codex login` has not been completed on this machine, a dispatch fails with `401 Unauthorized` or `not authenticated` mid-round-trip. Run this check once per session, cache the result, and re-run it only if a dispatch fails with an auth error.
73: 
74: ```bash
75: # One-shot pre-flight: capture ChatGPT OAuth status for routing
76: CODEX_AUTH=$(codex login status 2>&1)
77: echo "$CODEX_AUTH" | grep -qi "logged in\|chatgpt-oauth" && CODEX_OAUTH_OK=1 || CODEX_OAUTH_OK=0
78: ```
79: 
80: **Decision tree** (apply in order — first match wins):
81: 
82: | State | CODEX_OAUTH_OK | Action |
83: |-------|----------------|--------|
84: | OAuth ready | 1 | Proceed with `codex exec --model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium" -c service_tier="fast"` |
85: | Not logged in | 0 | **ASK user** to run `codex login` — surface the command, do NOT dispatch. Never substitute an API key or a different model. |
86: 
87: **User prompt template — not logged in:**
88: 
89: ```
90: Codex is not authenticated on this machine. cli-codex uses ChatGPT OAuth only.
91: Run `codex login` (browser flow; requires a ChatGPT Plus/Pro/Business/Edu/Enterprise account),
92: then confirm when login finishes — the skill will retry the original dispatch.
93: ```
94: 
95: **Error-recovery contract.** If a dispatch returns an auth error after pre-flight passed (OAuth expired or revoked), invalidate the cache, rerun `codex login`, and re-check before retrying. Never substitute a model the user didn't approve.
96: 
97: ### Default Invocation (Skill Default)
98: 
99: **Default model + effort + tier**: `gpt-5.5` · `medium` reasoning · `fast` service tier. Balances speed, cost, and quality for the typical delegation.
100: 
101: > **Fan-out fallback:** a deep-loop lineage that pins no model runs **GPT Luna**. The family is named here on purpose, without a version or an effort tier, so this line does not go stale when the family ships a point release; the runner resolves the current id. A drift test keeps the two in the same family.
102: 
103: ```bash
104: codex exec \
105:   --model gpt-5.5 \
106:   -c model_reasoning_effort="medium" \
107:   -c service_tier="fast" \
108:   -c approval_policy=never \
109:   --sandbox workspace-write \
110:   "<prompt>" </dev/null
111: ```
112: 
113: The trailing `</dev/null` is not optional in a non-interactive dispatch; Rule 6 below explains what a backgrounded codex does to an inherited stdin.
114: 
115: **User override** (honor explicit user phrasing verbatim):
116: 
117: | User says | Resolve to |
118: |-----------|------------|
119: | (nothing specified) | `--model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium" -c service_tier="fast"` |
120: | "Use gpt 5.5 high fast" | `--model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="high" -c service_tier="fast"` |
121: | "Use gpt 5.5 low" | `--model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="low" -c service_tier="fast"` (fast stays unless user drops it) |
122: | "Use gpt 5.5 xhigh" | `--model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="xhigh" -c service_tier="fast"` |
123: | "Use gpt 6 luna max" | `--model gpt-6-luna -c model_reasoning_effort="max" -c service_tier="fast"` |
124: | "Use gpt 5.6 terra high" | `--model gpt-5.6-terra -c model_reasoning_effort="high" -c service_tier="fast"` |
125: | "Use gpt 6.1 terra high" | `--model gpt-6.1-terra -c model_reasoning_effort="high" -c service_tier="fast"` |
126: | "Use gpt 6 sol ultra" | `--model gpt-6-sol -c model_reasoning_effort="ultra" -c service_tier="fast"` |
127: 
128: Honor whichever dimensions the user names. Model stays on `gpt-5.5` and service tier stays on `fast` unless the user explicitly names a different model or tier; keep the reasoning effort within the chosen model's ceiling (see Model Selection below and the roster in [references/providers-and-models.md](references/providers-and-models.md)).
129: 
130: ### Model Selection
131: 
132: `gpt-5.5` at `medium` on the `fast` service tier (`-c service_tier="fast"`) is the skill default for cross-AI delegation.
133: Alternates are `gpt-6-luna` (≤ `max`), and `gpt-5.6-terra`, `gpt-6.1-terra` and `gpt-6-sol` (≤ `ultra`).
134: [references/providers-and-models.md](references/providers-and-models.md) holds the full roster, the per-model effort ceilings and the 8-level effort ladder.
135: Set effort with `-c model_reasoning_effort="<level>"`. There is **no `--reasoning-effort` flag**.
136: 
137: **Selection Strategy**: default `gpt-5.5 medium`; raise to `high` / `xhigh` for architecture, security, and complex planning; escalate the model when the task wants reasoning past `xhigh`; drop to `low` / `minimal` for trivial lookups. Per-task rationale table: [cli-reference.md](./references/cli-reference.md) §5.
138: 
139: ### Codex Agent Delegation
140: 
141: The calling AI is the conductor; Codex profiles in `$CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml` shape HOW Codex processes the task (sandbox, reasoning). Route with `-p <name>` when the task matches a specialization. Full roster and invocation patterns: [agent-delegation.md](./references/agent-delegation.md).
142: 
143: | Task Type | Profile |
144: |-----------|---------|
145: | Code review / security audit | `review` |
146: | Architecture exploration | `context` |
147: | Technical research | `research` (+ top-level `--search`) |
148: | Documentation generation | `write` |
149: | Fresh-perspective debugging | `debug` |
150: | Multi-strategy planning | `ai-council` |
151: 
152: Git diff review uses the built-in subcommand (no `-p`): `codex exec review "..." --commit HEAD`. Profiles may override `model`, `model_reasoning_effort`, `sandbox_mode`, `approval_policy`. The `.codex/agents/*.toml` files define personas for the interactive multi-agent TUI, NOT the `-p` flag.
153: 
154: ### Dispatch-Critical Gotchas
155: 
156: The full flag glossary, sandbox modes, unique capabilities (`/review`, `--search`, `codex mcp`, session resume/fork, `--image`, `codex cloud`), essential command examples, and troubleshooting table are in the ALWAYS-loaded [cli-reference.md](./references/cli-reference.md). Five gotchas that break a dispatch, or make a child misreport its result, and must be honored at routing time:
157: 
158: - **`codex exec` defaults to `--sandbox read-only`** — file-modification tasks silently no-op (the agent plans changes but cannot write them). Pass `--sandbox workspace-write`; for headless no-prompt execution use top-level `-a never` before `exec` or `-c approval_policy=never`.
159: - **`--search` is a top-level flag, not an `exec` flag.** Enable live web search as `codex --search exec …`, because it precedes the subcommand.
160:   On codex ≥ 0.144 `codex exec --search` hard-fails with `unexpected argument '--search'`, and older 0.125 builds accepted it, so treat any `exec … --search` example as stale.
161:   Without it, `codex exec` has no web access and answers from training data only. Every dispatch needing live data (latest versions, repo facts, advisories) MUST use `codex --search exec …`.
162: - **Always pass `-c service_tier="fast"` explicitly** — this routes through the fast tier instead of whatever the caller's `~/.codex/config.toml` defaults to. Explicit means reproducible regardless of who runs it.
163: - **No `--reasoning-effort`, `--reasoning`, or `--quiet` flag exists** — set effort with `-c model_reasoning_effort="<level>"`; capture the last message with `-o file.txt`; capture stderr with `2>&1`.
164: - **`--sandbox workspace-write` blocks local IPC sockets, so a child cannot run checks that start `tsx`.** spec-kit's `npm --prefix runtime/cli run check` fails there with `listen EPERM`, and it also fails with `TMPDIR` pointed elsewhere. It passes outside the sandbox. That was observed 2026-09-24 on codex-cli 0.156.1.
165:   Tell the child which checks to leave to you, run them in the orchestrating session after it returns, and read that EPERM as a sandbox limit, not a code failure.
166: 
167: ---
168: 
169: ## 4. RULES
170: 
171: ### ✅ ALWAYS
172: 
173: 1. Verify Codex CLI is installed before first invocation (`command -v codex`).
174: 2. Delegate research and review lineages to `../../system-deep-loop/runtime/scripts/fanout-run.cjs` with executor kind `cli-codex`. It rejects every other loop type, so a single build or doc dispatch uses the child dispatch envelope in [providers-and-models.md](./references/providers-and-models.md) §5. Never build a second adapter in this packet.
175: 3. Use `--sandbox read-only` for review/analysis/research; `--sandbox workspace-write` for code generation/file modification — `codex exec` defaults to `read-only`, so omitting it causes silent no-op on edit tasks. For unattended approval, put top-level `-a never` before `exec` or set `-c approval_policy=never`.
176: 4. Validate Codex-generated code (XSS, injection, eval, syntax checks via `node --check`, `tsc --noEmit`, etc.) before applying.
177: 5. Capture stderr (`2>&1`) so rate-limit messages and errors surface.
178: 6. **Redirect codex stdin from `/dev/null` on EVERY non-interactive dispatch**, not only inside a `while read` loop. Pattern: `codex exec "$PROMPT" > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &`.
179:    Without `</dev/null`, the backgrounded codex process inherits the loop's stdin, the file after `done < input.jsonl`, and silently consumes the remaining lines. The loop then exits after 3-6 iterations with no error.
180:    See `references/integration-patterns.md#background-execution` → "Silent Stdin Consumption".
181: 7. **Specify model + effort + service tier explicitly** — never rely on caller environment. Default: `--model gpt-5.5 -c model_reasoning_effort="medium" -c service_tier="fast"`. Honor user overrides verbatim. Use `high`/`xhigh` for reasoning-heavy tasks (architecture, security, deep planning).
182: 8. Route to the appropriate `-p <profile>` when the task matches a specialization (see Section 3 routing table); use `codex exec review` (built-in subcommand) for git diff reviews.
183: 9. **Pass the spec folder to the delegated agent** in the prompt: if the calling AI has an active Gate-3 spec folder, include `Spec folder: <path> (pre-approved, skip Gate 3)`. If none, ASK the user before delegating — the delegated agent cannot answer Gate 3 in non-interactive mode.
184: 10. **Prompt construction & model-craft (cli-* family precedence).** Compose every dispatch prompt via the 2-tier rule canonical in `../../sk-prompt/assets/cli-prompt-quality-card.md`:
185:    1. **Fast path (default).** Build from the local `assets/prompt-quality-card.md`, which delegates the framework table + CLEAR check to the canonical card.
186:    2. **Deep path (escalation).** Dispatch `@prompt-improver` via the Task tool (never load full `sk-prompt` inline) when any canonical **Tier 2** trigger applies — the trigger list lives in `../../sk-prompt/assets/cli-prompt-quality-card.md` under "Tier 2 — Deep path"; do not re-enumerate it here.
187: 11. **Never inject user-level voice/personalization content into AI-orchestrated Codex delegations.** Codex CLI reads user-level voice from `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`, the human's global settings, loaded automatically.
188:    When an AI delegates via `codex exec`, the calling AI's own voice rules govern the response. Do NOT read `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` and paste it into delegation prompts.
189:    Keep delegations focused on task/model/sandbox/effort/(spec-folder pre-approval).
190:    If the user asks how to make Codex sound more like Claude in *their own* sessions, point to `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`, not any repo asset.
191: 12. **Code Standards Loading (surface-aware contract).** When you dispatch for code review or code generation, instruct the dispatched session to work these four steps in order.
192:    - Load `sk-code`.
193:    - Let `sk-code` emit a surface tag matching the detected stack from markers and target files.
194:    - Load the selected surface resources and run its verification commands.
195:    - Add `code-review` only for formal findings-first review output.
196:    Fallback: if the surface cannot be determined confidently, ask for the runtime surface and verification command set. NEVER hardcode obsolete sibling code skills in dispatch prompts.
197: 13. **Design Standards Loading (measured-reference contract).** When you dispatch for design or UI work, instruct the dispatched session to work these three steps in order.
198:    - Load `sk-design-md-generator`.
199:    - Extract a measured Style Reference DESIGN.md from the live source before building UI. It carries named color tokens, a type scale, components and Quick-Start CSS/Tailwind.
200:    - Build against those measured tokens and run the extraction's validate step to confirm hex/section fidelity.
201:    Fallback: if there is no live source to measure, ask for the reference URL or the exact tokens to build against. NEVER treat `mcp-figma` or `sk-design-md-generator` as a taste, visual-direction, or critique authority. The extraction measures real CSS. It does not judge design.
202: 14. **Pass the design reference manifest to the dispatched session.** When you dispatch design or UI work, inline a `DESIGN_DISPATCH_MANIFEST v1` block in the prompt, because the child cannot resolve skill paths and the manifest must travel in the payload rather than by reference. The block carries these fields:
203:    - `styleReferenceExtracted`, set true;
204:    - the live `source` that was measured;
205:    - the measured design tokens, type scale and components the child must build against;
206:    - `loadedFiles`;
207:    - `proofDemandBack`.
208:    If the manifest cannot be assembled, because no Style Reference was extracted or no live source was there to measure, ASK before launching the child rather than starting a silent design dispatch. The child returns the demanded proof. The parent reconciles it on the return path.
209: 15. **Single-dispatch discipline (operator-gated, session-scoped).** The default is ONE cli-* dispatch at a time across the cli-* family (cli-codex, cli-opencode, cli-claude-code). Wait for the dispatched agent's work to return, verify outputs exist, then SIGKILL only the dispatch THIS skill started.
210:    - Capture the PID at launch with `codex exec ... & CODEX_PID=$!`, then kill that captured PID directly plus its own orphan children with `kill -9 "$CODEX_PID" 2>/dev/null; pkill -9 -P "$CODEX_PID" 2>/dev/null`, then apply the same PID-scoped `gtimeout` cleanup.
211:    - **Never use a blanket `pkill -9 -f "codex exec --model"` pattern.** That matches and kills EVERY running `codex exec` process on the machine, including the operator's unrelated codex sessions.
212:    - Launch the next dispatch, this skill or a sibling, only after the prior one is dead and RSS has dropped.
213:    - **Within a deep-flow session** (deep-review / deep-research), the operator authorizes the whole multi-iteration session at start. Iterations chain back-to-back with kill-between as the safety mechanism, not a per-iteration confirmation prompt.
214:    - **Exception (cross-skill parallel).** When the operator explicitly authorizes N parallel dispatches, run N concurrently, but still SIGKILL each by its own captured PID as its work returns.
215: 16. **Set `AI_SESSION_CHILD=1` in the dispatched child's env AND state the exemption in the prompt.** The variable makes the waiver true. It does not make it observable.
216:    The reader being waived is a model, and a model cannot see an environment variable, so a child given only the variable still stops to ask the documentation-scope question and writes nothing, at exit code zero.
217:    Copy the preamble from [`shared/references/child-dispatch-preamble.md`](../shared/references/child-dispatch-preamble.md) to the top of every non-interactive prompt.
218:    A session may be launched through the per-session worktree wrapper (`.skilled/bin/worktree-session.sh`). A dispatched `codex exec` is an orchestrated sub-session, not a new top-level session, so it must SHARE the parent's worktree rather than allocate its own.
219:    The wrapper checks `AI_SESSION_CHILD`, plus a `git --git-common-dir` structural backstop, and exec's in place when the variable is set. Pattern: `AI_SESSION_CHILD=1 codex exec ... </dev/null`. This is harmless when the wrapper is not in use.
220:    See `.skilled/bin/README.md` → "Worktree session isolation".
221: 
222: 17. **Agent-persona injection (attach identity, not just the task).** Every dispatch composes `{resolved agent persona + task prompt}`. It never sends a bare task.
223:    - Resolve the persona from the ACTIVE runtime's agent directory per AGENTS.md §9 (`.skilled/agents/<name>.md`, `.claude/agents/<name>.md`, etc.), and never hardcode one runtime.
224:    - Map each subtask to the RIGHT agent (`code`→code, `review`→review, `design`→design, research→`deep-research`, docs→`markdown`), not to one default.
225:    - **Codex has no native persona surface.** `.codex/agents/*.toml` is TUI-only, and `codex exec` and `-p <profile>` load sandbox/effort config rather than a persona. So **INLINE** the persona block into the prompt payload on every dispatch, using the same in-payload pattern as the `DESIGN_DISPATCH_MANIFEST` in Rule 14, because the child cannot resolve agent paths by reference.
226:    - A persona-less dispatch runs the leaf as a generic assistant, silently dropping the agent's tool-scope, verification gates, and output contract.
227:    Canonical contract: `../../sk-prompt/assets/cli-prompt-quality-card.md` "Persona Injection". Native precedent: `orchestrate.md` "Agent Loading Protocol". Rare exceptions (focused summary for a small-context model, pure-mechanical command) are declared at the dispatch site.
228: 
229: 18. **Never dispatch `codex exec` from inside a running codex session.** A codex process cannot spawn another codex from inside its own sandbox.
230:    The nested child dies at startup with `failed to initialize in-process app-server client: Operation not permitted`, observed 2026-09-02 on codex-cli 0.151.0 under `--sandbox workspace-write`.
231:    The parent reads that as a failed iteration rather than a route violation. So when codex is itself the executor of a deep-loop fan-out lineage or any other orchestrating session, it must do each iteration's work in-process with its own tools and never dispatch a second codex.
232:    Grep that exact message to confirm you are hitting this and not a model or network fault.
233: 
234: ### ⛔ NEVER
235: 
236: 1. Use `--sandbox danger-full-access` without explicit user approval (full shell beyond workspace = damage risk). A no-prompt approval policy does not remove the need for explicit scope approval.
237: 2. Trust Codex output blindly for security-sensitive code, send sensitive data (API keys, passwords, credentials) in prompts, or hammer the API with rapid sequential calls.
238: 3. Use Codex for tasks where context is already loaded — direct action by the calling AI is faster.
239: 4. Assume Codex output is correct without verification — cross-reference codebase and project standards.
240: 5. Build or maintain a packet-local Codex execution adapter; the deep-loop runtime is the execution authority.
241: 
242: ### ⚠️ ESCALATE IF
243: 
244: 1. Codex CLI is not installed and user has not acknowledged (provide `npm i -g @openai/codex`).
245: 2. Rate limits are persistently exceeded (suggest checking the ChatGPT OAuth account's plan and usage limits).
246: 3. Codex output conflicts with existing code patterns (present both perspectives; user decides).
247: 4. Task requires `--sandbox danger-full-access` (describe risks; get explicit user approval). A no-prompt approval policy still requires explicit scope approval.
248: 
249: ### Memory Handback Protocol
250: 
251: When the calling AI needs to preserve session context from a Codex CLI delegation, run the canonical procedure: extract the `MEMORY_HANDBACK` section, build structured JSON, scrub secrets, and invoke `generate-context.js` via `--stdin`/`--json`/temp-file. The continuity writer is the last step, and nothing is handed to an index.
252: Full procedure and caveats: [`system-spec-kit/references/cli/memory-handback.md`](../../system-spec-kit/references/cli/memory-handback.md). Codex-specific Memory Epilogue template: [assets/prompt-templates.md](./assets/prompt-templates.md) §13.
253: 
254: ```bash
255: printf '%s' "$JSON_PAYLOAD" | node .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/cli/dist/continuity/generate-context.js --stdin [spec-folder]
256: ```
257: 
258: ---
259: 
260: ## 5. REFERENCES
261: 
262: ### Core References
263: 
264: - [cli-reference.md](./references/cli-reference.md) - Complete CLI subcommands, flags, sandbox modes, and config reference
265: - [integration-patterns.md](./references/integration-patterns.md) - Cross-AI orchestration patterns and workflows

271: 
272: - [prompt-templates.md](./assets/prompt-templates.md) - Copy-paste ready prompt templates for common tasks
273: - [prompt-quality-card.md](./assets/prompt-quality-card.md) - Fast-path prompt framework + CLEAR check (ALWAYS loaded)

276: 
277: - [shared-smart-router.md](../../system-spec-kit/references/cli/shared-smart-router.md) - Helper-function bodies for the smart router.
278: - [memory-handback.md](../../system-spec-kit/references/cli/memory-handback.md) - Canonical 7-step Memory Handback procedure.
279: 
280: ### External
281: 
282: - [Codex CLI GitHub](https://github.com/openai/codex) - Official repository
283: - [OpenAI ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com) - ChatGPT OAuth account (auth for cli-codex)
284: 
285: ### Reference Loading Notes
286: 
287: - Load only references needed for current intent. [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) is the single routing authority.
288: - `cli-reference.md` is ALWAYS loaded as baseline.
289: 
290: ---
291: 
292: ## 6. SUCCESS CRITERIA
293: 
294: ### Task Completion
295: 
296: - Codex CLI invoked with correct subcommand, flags, model, and sandbox mode.
297: - Output captured, validated, and integrated appropriately; no security vulnerabilities introduced.
298: - Rate limits handled gracefully (retry or fallback strategy).
299: - Appropriate Codex profile and sandbox level matched to task type (read-only for review, workspace-write for generation).
300: - Orchestrated execution delegated to the shared deep-loop runtime without a packet-local adapter.
301: 
302: ### Skill Quality
303: 
304: - All 9 sections present with proper anchor comments.
305: - Smart routing covers all intent signals with UNKNOWN_FALLBACK.
306: - Reference files provide deep-dive content without duplication.
307: 
308: ---
309: 
310: ## 7. INTEGRATION POINTS
311: 
312: ### Framework Integration
313: 
314: This skill operates within the behavioral framework defined in [AGENTS.md](../../../../AGENTS.md).
315: 
316: Key integrations:
317: - **Gate 2**: Skill routing via `skill_advisor.py`
318: - **Tool Routing**: Per AGENTS.md Section 5 decision tree
319: - **Continuity**: Context preserved by `/speckit:save`, which writes through `generate-context.js`
320: - **Execution**: Shared deep-loop runtime (`../../system-deep-loop/runtime/scripts/fanout-run.cjs`)

322: **Tool roles**: Bash dispatches the CLI; Read/Glob/Grep validate output.
323: 
324: ---

326: ## 8. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
327: 
328: The router discovers reference, asset, and script docs dynamically (Section 5 is the authored index). Start with the ALWAYS-loaded `references/cli-reference.md` and `assets/prompt-quality-card.md`, then load task-specific resources per [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md).

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.

136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).

146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.

12: ---
13: 
14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
159: 
160: Copy this scaffold, then remove sections that do not apply.
161: 
162: ````markdown
163: ---
164: title: "[PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]"
165: description: "[One-sentence description]"

241:

243: |---|---|

14: # SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide
15: 
16: Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
90: > Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
91: > Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).
92: 
93: ### Template
94: 
95: ```yaml
96: ---
97: name: sk-example
98: description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
99: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
100: version: 1.0.0.0
101: ---
102: ```
103: 
104: ### Key Rules
105: 
106: - **name**: Must match folder name exactly, hyphen-case only
107: - **description**: Third-person voice, single line, no `<>` brackets
108: - **allowed-tools**: Use brackets `[...]`, not comma-separated string
109: - **hard rules**: Not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects the dispatch preflight reads.
110: 
111: > **Complete Reference**: For validation rules, edge cases, array formats, and all document type frontmatter, see [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md)
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 3. SKILL TEMPLATE (WITH BUNDLED RESOURCES)
116: 
117: **Use for**: Skills with bundled resources (references, scripts, or assets)
118: 
119: **Target**: 800-2000 lines (SKILL.md <1000 lines, rest in resources)

413: - Section 1 (WHEN TO USE): 150-200 lines
414: - Section 2 (SMART ROUTING): 8-12 non-blank lines of plain prose (the router block lives in the sibling `ROUTER.md`)
415: - Section 3 (HOW IT WORKS): 200-300 lines
416: - Section 4 (RULES): 150-200 lines
417: - Section 5 (REFERENCES): 40-120 lines
418: - Section 6 (SUCCESS CRITERIA): 80-120 lines
419: - Section 7 (INTEGRATION POINTS): 100-150 lines
420: - Section 8 (REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES): 20-60 lines

422: **Bundled Resources Structure (Monolithic)**:
423: ```
424: .skilled/skills/skill-name/       # Note: .skilled/skills/ (singular, NOT skills)
425: ├── SKILL.md (800-1000 lines)
426: └── Bundled Resources
427:     ├── scripts/          - Executable automation
428:     ├── references/       - Detailed documentation (flat or domain subfolders)
429:     └── assets/           - Templates and examples (subfolders OK)
430:         ├── opencode/     - OpenCode component templates (skills, agents, commands)
431:         └── readme/        - README-shaped scaffolds (README, install guide)
432: ```

434: **Folder Organization Principle**:
435: - **references/** = flat for small skills, domain subfolders for medium/complex skills
436:   - Flat example: `references/core-standards.md`, `references/validation.md`
437:   - Domain example: `references/backend/go/`, `references/frontend/react/`
438: - **assets/** = Subfolders ALLOWED when organizing many files by category
439:   - Group related templates together
440:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
441: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections

443: **Native Discovery**:
444: - Skills auto-discovered from `.skilled/skills/*/SKILL.md` frontmatter
445: - Skill name in frontmatter MUST match folder name
446: - Skills appear as `skills_<name>` functions in OpenCode (hyphens → underscores)

504: ### Section 2: SMART ROUTING (Required for All Skills)
505: 
506: **Purpose**: Use this section to explain how you route a request to this skill's resources.
507: 
508: **Three skill kinds, one shape**:
509: 
510: | Kind | How to tell | What Section 2 says |
511: |------|-------------|---------------------|
512: | Hub | the folder holds `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` | how a prompt reaches a mode, and where the root `ROUTER.md` is |
513: | Mode packet | a packet folder inside a hub | what selects this packet, what it loads first, and where its own `ROUTER.md` is |
514: | Standalone | neither hub file | the same as a mode packet, with the router in its own `ROUTER.md` |
515: 
516: **The limit**: 12 non-blank lines and 180 words are the hard ceilings the check enforces. Aim for 8 to 12 lines. A packet or standalone skill says three things: what selects it, what it loads first, and where the machine router is.
517: 
518: **The sibling router**: the machine router lives in `ROUTER.md` beside `SKILL.md`, under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading.
519: That heading is the one every reader parses. Its section number is optional, so `## MACHINE ROUTER` and `## 9. MACHINE ROUTER` both count, and the check ignores the number.
520: Keep pseudocode out of SMART ROUTING and put it in that section.
521: `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own: two homes for one router is the dual declaration the check reports.
522: 
523: **The link line**: Section 2 names the router file with a relative markdown link, [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md), and its target resolves on disk. A sentence that mentions the name without a link fails, because a reader cannot follow it to a file that is not there.
524: 
525: **One router per folder**: every skill and every mode packet owns `ROUTER.md` inside its own folder, linked from its own `SKILL.md`. A router file whose real path leaves the folder is not that skill's router.
526: 
527: **The no-match outcome** is named `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` everywhere. Low confidence returns a disambiguation checklist, never an empty result and never a guess.
528: 
529: **Validation**: `package_skill.py --strict` reports the routing shape with five codes:
530: 
531: | Code | Finding |
532: |------|---------|
533: | `RS-001` | SMART ROUTING is longer than the limit (12 lines or 180 words by default) |
534: | `RS-002` | `SKILL.md` carries a `## MACHINE ROUTER` section, with or without a code block |
535: | `RS-003` | A `## MACHINE ROUTER` section is not the last H2 of the document that holds it |
536: | `RS-004` | the skill has no sibling `ROUTER.md`, or its real path leaves the skill folder |
537: | `RS-005` | `SKILL.md` has no relative markdown link to `./ROUTER.md` that resolves |
538: 
539: The machine block itself is a fenced block or an unfenced run of indented lines.
540: It declares the router with one of these markers: `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `DEFAULT_RESOURCE =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`.
541: A fence closes only on a run of the same character that is at least as long as its opening run.
542: 
543: **Known debt** is listed in `sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`.
544: Entries use skill paths relative to `.skilled/skills`, such as `sk-code/sk-code-review`.
545: A folder outside that root is never debt.
546: Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`.
547: A listed skill fails if its line count, word count or machine blocks left in `SKILL.md` exceed the record, or if it adds an unrecorded code.
548: The checker ignores entries in any other form.
549: Remove an entry when the skill follows the canon.
550: 
551: **Placement**: the SMART ROUTING section sits after Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) and before HOW IT WORKS, and `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md` at the skill root.
552: 
553: **Worked example** (a canon Section 2 and its sibling router, nothing else):
554: 
555: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
556: 
557: Use this skill for [domain] work: [trigger 1], [trigger 2], or [trigger 3].
558: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
559: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. The other files assume it.
560: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.
561: Keep every path inside this skill folder and load a file only when it exists.
562: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
563: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
564: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md); read it before selecting a resource.
565: 
566: ---
567: 
568: The link resolves to the sibling file, whose one heading the readers parse is:
569: 
570: \## MACHINE ROUTER
571: 
572: ```python
573: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/[default].md"
574: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"PRIMARY": {"weight": 4, "keywords": [("[keyword]", 4), ("[phrase]", 3)]}}
575: RESOURCE_MAP = {"PRIMARY": ["references/[domain]/[primary].md"]}
576: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = ["Confirm the routing key", "Confirm the intent", "Provide one concrete input"]
577: 
578: def route_[skill_name]_resources(user_request, task=None):
579:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
580:     primary, secondary, scores = classify_intents(user_request, task)
581:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 0.5:
582:         return {"load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK", "checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST}
583:     return {"routing_key": get_routing_key(task, [primary]), "resources": inventory}
584: ```
585: 
586: The full resilience pattern (guarded paths, recursive discovery, routing keys) is in [skill-smart-router.md](./skill-smart-router.md).
587: 
588: **Writing Tips**:
589: - Open Section 2 with the signal that actually picks this skill's files.
590: - Name the first file to load, so a reader knows where to start.
591: - Name the router file with a markdown link, so a reader can open it.
592: - Keep `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` as the named no-match outcome.
593: - Edit `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` in `ROUTER.md` when the skill gains a domain.
594: - Avoid duplicate lookup tables, static file inventories, and unguarded `load()` calls.
595: 
596: **Word Budget**: 8-12 non-blank lines of prose

14: # SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide
15: 
16: Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
90: > Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
91: > Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).
92: 
93: ### Template
94: 
95: ```yaml
96: ---
97: name: sk-example
98: description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
99: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
100: version: 1.0.0.0
101: ---
102: ```
103: 
104: ### Key Rules
105: 
106: - **name**: Must match folder name exactly, hyphen-case only
107: - **description**: Third-person voice, single line, no `<>` brackets
108: - **allowed-tools**: Use brackets `[...]`, not comma-separated string
109: - **hard rules**: Not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects the dispatch preflight reads.
110: 
111: > **Complete Reference**: For validation rules, edge cases, array formats, and all document type frontmatter, see [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md)
112: 
113: ---

138: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]

510: | Kind | How to tell | What Section 2 says |
511: |------|-------------|---------------------|
512: | Hub | the folder holds `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` | how a prompt reaches a mode, and where the root `ROUTER.md` is |
513: | Mode packet | a packet folder inside a hub | what selects this packet, what it loads first, and where its own `ROUTER.md` is |
514: | Standalone | neither hub file | the same as a mode packet, with the router in its own `ROUTER.md` |
515: 
516: **The limit**: 12 non-blank lines and 180 words are the hard ceilings the check enforces. Aim for 8 to 12 lines. A packet or standalone skill says three things: what selects it, what it loads first, and where the machine router is.
517: 
518: **The sibling router**: the machine router lives in `ROUTER.md` beside `SKILL.md`, under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading.
519: That heading is the one every reader parses. Its section number is optional, so `## MACHINE ROUTER` and `## 9. MACHINE ROUTER` both count, and the check ignores the number.
520: Keep pseudocode out of SMART ROUTING and put it in that section.
521: `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own: two homes for one router is the dual declaration the check reports.
522: 
523: **The link line**: Section 2 names the router file with a relative markdown link, [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md), and its target resolves on disk. A sentence that mentions the name without a link fails, because a reader cannot follow it to a file that is not there.
524: 
525: **One router per folder**: every skill and every mode packet owns `ROUTER.md` inside its own folder, linked from its own `SKILL.md`. A router file whose real path leaves the folder is not that skill's router.
526: 
527: **The no-match outcome** is named `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` everywhere. Low confidence returns a disambiguation checklist, never an empty result and never a guess.
528: 
529: **Validation**: `package_skill.py --strict` reports the routing shape with five codes:
530: 
531: | Code | Finding |
532: |------|---------|
533: | `RS-001` | SMART ROUTING is longer than the limit (12 lines or 180 words by default) |
534: | `RS-002` | `SKILL.md` carries a `## MACHINE ROUTER` section, with or without a code block |
535: | `RS-003` | A `## MACHINE ROUTER` section is not the last H2 of the document that holds it |
536: | `RS-004` | the skill has no sibling `ROUTER.md`, or its real path leaves the skill folder |
537: | `RS-005` | `SKILL.md` has no relative markdown link to `./ROUTER.md` that resolves |
538: 
539: The machine block itself is a fenced block or an unfenced run of indented lines.
540: It declares the router with one of these markers: `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `DEFAULT_RESOURCE =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`.
541: A fence closes only on a run of the same character that is at least as long as its opening run.
542: 
543: **Known debt** is listed in `sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`.
544: Entries use skill paths relative to `.skilled/skills`, such as `sk-code/sk-code-review`.
545: A folder outside that root is never debt.
546: Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`.
547: A listed skill fails if its line count, word count or machine blocks left in `SKILL.md` exceed the record, or if it adds an unrecorded code.
548: The checker ignores entries in any other form.
549: Remove an entry when the skill follows the canon.
550: 
551: **Placement**: the SMART ROUTING section sits after Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) and before HOW IT WORKS, and `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md` at the skill root.
552: 
553: **Worked example** (a canon Section 2 and its sibling router, nothing else):
554: 
555: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
556: 
557: Use this skill for [domain] work: [trigger 1], [trigger 2], or [trigger 3].
558: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
559: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. The other files assume it.
560: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.
561: Keep every path inside this skill folder and load a file only when it exists.
562: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
563: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
564: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md); read it before selecting a resource.
565: 
566: ---
567: 
568: The link resolves to the sibling file, whose one heading the readers parse is:
569: 
570: \## MACHINE ROUTER
571: 
572: ```python
573: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/[default].md"
574: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"PRIMARY": {"weight": 4, "keywords": [("[keyword]", 4), ("[phrase]", 3)]}}
575: RESOURCE_MAP = {"PRIMARY": ["references/[domain]/[primary].md"]}
576: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = ["Confirm the routing key", "Confirm the intent", "Provide one concrete input"]
577: 
578: def route_[skill_name]_resources(user_request, task=None):
579:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
580:     primary, secondary, scores = classify_intents(user_request, task)
581:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 0.5:
582:         return {"load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK", "checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST}
583:     return {"routing_key": get_routing_key(task, [primary]), "resources": inventory}
584: ```
585: 
586: The full resilience pattern (guarded paths, recursive discovery, routing keys) is in [skill-smart-router.md](./skill-smart-router.md).
587: 
588: **Writing Tips**:
589: - Open Section 2 with the signal that actually picks this skill's files.
590: - Name the first file to load, so a reader knows where to start.
591: - Name the router file with a markdown link, so a reader can open it.
592: - Keep `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` as the named no-match outcome.
593: - Edit `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` in `ROUTER.md` when the skill gains a domain.
594: - Avoid duplicate lookup tables, static file inventories, and unguarded `load()` calls.
595: 
596: **Word Budget**: 8-12 non-blank lines of prose
597: 
598: ---

14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations
97: - Anti-patterns to avoid
98: 
99: **Use cases**:
100: - Complete skill applications
101: - Common patterns
102: - Edge cases
103: - Quality standards
104: 
105: ### Guide Files
106: **Purpose**: Detailed how-to guides for complex processes
107: 
108: **Naming**: `[process]-guide.md`
109: - Example: `packaging-guide.md`, `distribution-guide.md`
110: 
111: **Structure**:
112: - Step-by-step instructions
113: - Troubleshooting sections
114: - Best practices
115: - Common pitfalls
116: 
117: **Use cases**:
118: - Multi-step processes
119: - Advanced techniques
120: - Workflow deep-dives
121: - Integration guides
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |
227: 
228: ---
229: 
230: ## 4. STANDARD ASSET STRUCTURE
231: 
232: **Template**:
233: 
234: ````markdown
235: ---
236: title: Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
237: description: One-line description of what this asset provides
238: trigger_phrases:
239:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
240:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
241:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
242: importance_tier: normal
243: contextType: general
244: version: 1.0.0.0
245: ---
246: 
247: # Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
248:

250: 
251: \## 1. OVERVIEW
252: 
253: ### Purpose
254: 
255: [Why this asset exists, what problem it solves]
256: 
257: ### Usage
258: 
259: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
260: 
261: ---
262: 
263: \## 2. SECTION NAME
264: 
265: **Key Points**:
266: - Point 1
267: - Point 2
268: - Point 3
269: 
270: **Template**:
271: ```[language]
272: # Template content here
273: # With explanatory comments
274: ```
275: 
276: **Field Guidelines**:
277: 
278: **`field_name`**:
279: - Description of field
280: - Format requirements
281: - Example: `value-example`
282: 
283: **Complete Example**:
284: ```[language]
285: # Complete working example
286: # Ready to copy and adapt
287: ```
288: 
289: ---
290: 
291: \## 3. SECTION NAME
292: 
293: [Continue pattern...]
294: 
295: ---
296: 
297: ## N. RELATED RESOURCES
298: 
299: [Links to related files - MUST be last section if present]
300: 
301: ````
